newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Citra Marga sees higher net in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Citra Marga sees higher net in 1997.

text.p: Indonesian toll-road operator PT Citra Marga Nusaphala Persada said on Tuesday it expected to book net profit of 154 billion rupiah in 1997, up from 123.6 billion rupiah in 1996, because of an increase in road traffic.
The company, controlled by Siti Hardianti Rukmana, the eldest daughter of President Suharto, said the higher net profit would be reached without any increase in toll fees.
Company finance director Tito Sulistio told reporters after a shareholders meeting that the projection had been raised from a previous projection of 145 billion rupiah in January.
The meeting also approved a dividend payment of 51 rupiah per share for 1996 and the issue of one-for-one rights in July at 500 rupiah per share to raise 500 billion rupiah.
Sulistio said the proceeds of the rights issue would be wholly used to finance the construction of a 36.5-km toll road in East Java.

The company has said total investment in the project was 1.3 trillion rupiah, and would be financed by the proceeds of a 275 billion rupiah bond, a 300 billion rupiah Eurobond, the 500 billion rupiah proceeds from the rights issue and internal funding.
Construction of the toll road project will start by the end of 1997 and it will be in operation by 2001.
Citra Marga's director of operations Bambang Soeroso said the company would achieve the 1997 target although it has no plans to to propose a toll increase this year.
He said Citra Marga would book higher net profits in 1997 on higher traffic from a new toll road connecting Jakarta's Tanjung Priok port to the industrial area in the city.

"We are very optimistic that our profit this year will increase significantly due to higher traffic on that new toll-road," Soeroso said adding that the annual growth of road traffic was about 16 to 17 percent in Jakarta.
Soeroso also said the firm was planning to expand business overseas including in Beijing, South Africa and in three eastern European countries -- Poland, Hungaria and Romania.
"So far, we have not come to any decision whether we are going to invest in the road network or offer management expertise in those countries," Soeroso said.
